true: A converging lens forms an inverted real image on the opposite side when the object lies beyond its focal point.
false: A converging lens forms an upright real image on the opposite side when the object lies beyond its focal point.

true: An object inside a converging lens's focal length produces an upright, magnified virtual image on the object's side.
false: An object inside a converging lens's focal length produces an upright, magnified virtual image on the lens's opposite side.

true: Parallel rays entering an ideal converging thin lens meet at its focal plane after refraction through the lens.
false: Parallel rays entering any real converging lens meet at one identical focal point regardless of their wavelength.

true: The thin-lens equation relates focal length to object and image distances measured from the lens's principal plane.
false: The thin-lens equation relates focal length to object and image distances measured from the lens's nearest surface.

true: Linear magnification equals image height divided by object height, with a negative sign convention indicating an inverted image.
false: Linear magnification equals image height divided by object height, with a positive sign convention indicating an inverted image.

true: For a real object, a diverging lens creates a reduced, upright virtual image between the lens and its focal point.
false: For a real object, a diverging lens creates a magnified, upright virtual image between the lens and its focal point.

true: As an object approaches a converging lens's focal point from beyond it, the real image recedes and becomes larger.
false: As an object approaches a converging lens's focal point from beyond it, the real image approaches and becomes larger.

true: Narrowing an ideal lens aperture dims the image and increases depth of field without changing the paraxial image position.
false: Narrowing an ideal lens aperture dims the image and increases depth of field by lengthening the lens's focal length.

true: Independent events satisfy the rule that learning one event occurred leaves the probability of the other event unchanged.
false: Independent events satisfy the rule that learning one event occurred raises the probability of the opposite outcome for the other.

true: After any recorded streak of heads from independent fair flips, the next coin flip still has one-half probability of heads.
false: After any recorded streak of heads from independent fair flips, the next coin flip has increased probability of tails.

true: Ten consecutive heads have probability one in 1,024, but after nine heads the conditional chance of another remains one-half.
false: Ten consecutive heads have probability one in 1,024, so after nine heads the conditional chance of another is one in 1,024.

true: Long sequences of independent random outcomes naturally contain clusters and streaks, even when every trial uses the same probability.
false: Long sequences of independent random outcomes should distribute evenly, so visible clusters and streaks indicate changing trial probabilities.

true: Independent events need not be mutually exclusive; their joint occurrence equals the product of their individual probabilities.
false: Independent events must be mutually exclusive; their joint occurrence equals the product of their individual probabilities.

true: For independent events, the probability that both occur equals the product of their individual probabilities.
false: For independent events, the probability that both occur equals the sum of their individual probabilities.

true: Independence describes the generating process, so an observed streak creates no balancing tendency in later trials.
false: Independence describes the generating process, so an observed streak creates a balancing tendency in later trials.

true: Stopping only after a desired streak biases the reported dataset, although it leaves each independent trial's probability unchanged.
false: Stopping only after a desired streak biases each trial's underlying probability, increasing the physical frequency of the selected streak.

true: A broad index fund reduces company-specific risk by holding many securities, but it remains exposed to overall market declines.
false: A broad index fund eliminates company-specific and market risk by holding enough securities across many industries.

true: Lower annual fund fees preserve more capital for compounding, so small fee differences substantially affect long-term wealth.
false: Lower annual fund fees affect only the first year's return, so small fee differences barely influence long-term wealth.

true: An index fund seeks to track a benchmark before costs, leaving actual investor returns slightly different because of fees and tracking error.
false: An index fund exactly matches its benchmark after costs, because passive management removes fees and tracking error.

true: Picking a few individual stocks concentrates both potential gains and company-specific losses compared with owning a broad market index.
false: Picking a few researched individual stocks preserves potential gains while diversifying company-specific losses as effectively as a broad index.

true: Diversification reduces risks unique to particular companies, but it cannot prevent losses caused by a broad market downturn.
false: Diversification reduces risks unique to particular companies and prevents losses caused by a broad market downturn.

true: Frequent stock trading creates transaction costs and taxable gains that reduce an investor's return in a taxable account.
false: Frequent stock trading defers taxable gains and reduces transaction costs, improving an investor's return in a taxable account.

true: A market-cap-weighted index assigns larger weights to companies with greater market values and changes those weights as prices move.
false: A market-cap-weighted index assigns equal weights to every company and preserves those weights as prices move.

true: Passive investing follows predefined rules rather than avoiding all trades; index funds rebalance when their benchmark composition changes.
false: Passive investing avoids all trades after purchase; index funds retain every original holding even when their benchmark composition changes.

true: An octave sounds strongly consonant because its frequencies form a two-to-one ratio, aligning many harmonics between both notes.
false: An octave sounds strongly consonant because its frequencies form a three-to-one ratio, aligning many harmonics between both notes.

true: A pure perfect fifth uses a three-to-two frequency ratio, causing numerous upper partials of its two notes to coincide.
false: A pure perfect fifth uses a four-to-three frequency ratio, causing numerous upper partials of its two notes to coincide.

true: Dissonant roughness increases when nearby partials fall within the same auditory critical band and produce rapid beating.
false: Dissonant roughness increases when nearby partials coincide exactly within the same auditory critical band and eliminate beating.

true: Perceived consonance reflects frequency relationships, tone spectra, tuning, musical context, and learned expectations rather than one universal ratio rule.
false: Perceived consonance reflects frequency relationships alone, because simple integer ratios determine chord quality regardless of timbre or musical context.

true: Equal temperament makes a perfect fifth slightly narrower than the pure three-to-two interval, supporting consistent transposition among keys.
false: Equal temperament makes a perfect fifth slightly wider than the pure three-to-two interval, supporting consistent transposition among keys.

true: Inverting a chord preserves its pitch classes but changes the bass note, spacing, acoustical spectrum, and perceived stability.
false: Inverting a chord preserves its pitch classes and therefore leaves the bass function, acoustical spectrum, and perceived stability unchanged.

true: A major triad combines intervals whose lower harmonics substantially overlap, helping many listeners hear the chord as fused and stable.
false: A major triad combines intervals whose fundamental frequencies exactly belong to one harmonic series in equal temperament, ensuring perfect stability.

true: A tritone creates tension through acoustical roughness and learned voice-leading expectations, with its effect depending on voicing and context.
false: A tritone always creates identical tension through acoustical roughness alone, with its effect independent of voicing and musical context.

true: Yeast makes bread rise by fermenting sugars into carbon dioxide, which expands inside bubbles supported by the dough's gluten network.
false: Yeast makes bread rise by fermenting sugars into carbon dioxide, which starch granules trap more effectively than the dough's gluten network.

true: Baking soda leavens dough efficiently when an acid supplies protons, allowing bicarbonate reactions to release carbon dioxide gas.
false: Baking soda leavens dough efficiently without an acid, because bicarbonate releases the same carbon dioxide immediately in plain water.

true: Baking powder contains both a base and dry acids, producing carbon dioxide after moisture and, for double-acting types, heat activate it.
false: Baking powder contains both a base and dry acids, producing carbon dioxide only after oven heat activates every type.

true: Kneading develops a connected gluten network that stretches around gas cells, helping dough retain fermentation gases as it rises.
false: Kneading develops a connected gluten network that generates carbon dioxide as its proteins cross-link, directly causing the dough to rise.

true: Overproofed dough collapses when its expanded gluten structure becomes too weak to retain gas during handling or baking.
false: Overproofed dough collapses when yeast exhausts available sugar and stops producing gas, despite the expanded gluten structure remaining strong.

true: Early oven spring comes from expanding gases, water vapor, and temporarily faster yeast activity before heat kills the yeast.
false: Early oven spring comes from expanding gases, water vapor, and sustained yeast fermentation that continues until the crust fully forms.

true: Moderate salt strengthens wheat dough and slows yeast fermentation, helping control both gas production and the final crumb structure.
false: Moderate salt weakens wheat dough and accelerates yeast fermentation, helping maximize gas production and the final crumb structure.

true: Sourdough rises through gases produced by its microbial community, while yeasts and lactic acid bacteria also create characteristic flavors and acidity.
false: Sourdough rises mainly through carbon dioxide from lactic acid bacteria, while yeasts create acidity and contribute little leavening gas.

true: Vaccines expose the immune system to selected antigens, expanding specific lymphocyte clones without requiring the full natural disease.
false: Vaccines expose the immune system to selected antibodies, expanding specific lymphocyte clones without requiring the full natural disease.

true: After vaccination, some activated B and T cells become long-lived memory cells that respond faster during later exposure.
false: After vaccination, all activated B and T cells remain permanently active, continuously producing a maximal response until later exposure.

true: Protective immunity involves pathogen-specific combinations of neutralizing antibodies, helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells, and memory responses.
false: Protective immunity depends exclusively on circulating antibodies, because T cells cannot recognize cells infected by pathogens.

true: A booster dose reactivates memory lymphocytes, increasing antibody quantity, binding affinity, and the durability of protection.
false: A booster dose replaces memory lymphocytes with naive cells, increasing antibody quantity, binding affinity, and protection durability.

true: Vaccine immunity develops over days or weeks because lymphocytes must activate, multiply, differentiate, and establish memory.
false: Vaccine immunity becomes complete within minutes because injected antigens immediately transform into long-lived antibodies and memory cells.

true: Messenger RNA vaccines deliver temporary cytoplasmic instructions for an antigen; the RNA is subsequently broken down without entering the nucleus.
false: Messenger RNA vaccines deliver permanent nuclear instructions for an antigen; the RNA integrates into chromosomes before cells express it.

true: Vaccine adjuvants stimulate innate danger signals that strengthen adaptive responses, but they do not supply pathogen-specific antibodies themselves.
false: Vaccine adjuvants supply pathogen-specific antibodies directly, eliminating the need for innate signaling during development of adaptive responses.

true: Widespread vaccination reduces pathogen transmission and indirectly protects vulnerable people without guaranteeing zero infections among vaccinated individuals.
false: Widespread vaccination indirectly protects vulnerable people only by curing their infections after transmission, rather than reducing transmission.

true: A B-tree index accelerates selective equality and range filters by locating relevant keys without scanning every table row.
false: A B-tree index guarantees constant-time equality and range filters by locating every relevant key with a single comparison.

true: Indexes speed many reads but add storage and write overhead because inserts, updates, and deletes also modify index structures.
false: Indexes speed many reads without affecting writes because inserts, updates, and deletes modify only the underlying table rows.

true: A composite B-tree index on columns A and B supports filtering by A because A is its leading column.
false: A composite B-tree index on columns A and B supports filtering by B equally well because column order is irrelevant.

true: A covering index contains every column needed by a query, permitting execution without extra row lookups in the base table.
false: A covering index contains every row in physical table order, permitting execution without filtering or sorting for any query.

true: For a filter matching most rows, a table scan costs less than repeated random row lookups through an index.
false: For a filter matching most rows, an index scan costs less because indexes remain faster at every selectivity.

true: Without a matching expression index, filtering on LOWER(name) prevents direct lookup through a conventional index on untransformed name values.
false: Without a matching expression index, filtering on LOWER(name) uses a conventional index that automatically derives transformed name values.

true: Stale statistics that misrepresent data distribution produce inaccurate cardinality estimates and steer the query planner toward inefficient execution plans.
false: Query planners derive exact row counts directly from SQL text, so stale table and index statistics cannot affect execution plans.

true: An index whose key order matches a query's ordering avoids a separate sort while scanning rows in index order.
false: Any index on the queried table avoids a separate sort, regardless of its indexed columns or key order.

true: Greenhouse gases warm the lower atmosphere by absorbing and re-emitting outgoing infrared radiation, slowing Earth's loss of energy to space.
false: Greenhouse gases warm the lower atmosphere mainly by reflecting incoming visible sunlight downward, increasing Earth's absorbed solar energy.

true: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth's surface warmer than its airless radiative temperature, while added greenhouse gases enhance that warming.
false: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth's surface cooler than its airless radiative temperature, while added greenhouse gases reverse that cooling.

true: Carbon dioxide accumulates when emissions exceed natural removals, so its warming influence depends strongly on cumulative human emissions.
false: Carbon dioxide cannot accumulate because natural sinks remove each year's emissions completely, so warming depends only on current annual emissions.

true: Water vapor mainly amplifies current global warming as a feedback because warmer air supports more atmospheric moisture.
false: Water vapor initiates current global warming as an independent forcing because extra atmospheric moisture raises temperature before any other change.

true: Increasing carbon dioxide tends to warm the surface and troposphere while cooling the stratosphere, a characteristic greenhouse-gas pattern.
false: Increasing carbon dioxide tends to warm the surface, troposphere, and stratosphere equally, a characteristic greenhouse-gas pattern.

true: The greenhouse effect raises the average altitude from which infrared escapes, where colder air emits less energy until temperatures adjust upward.
false: The greenhouse effect lowers the average altitude from which infrared escapes, where warmer air emits less energy until temperatures adjust upward.

true: A cold day describes local short-term weather and does not contradict a long-term rise in global average temperature.
false: A cold day directly contradicts a long-term rise in global average temperature because climate is the average of daily weather.

true: Methane produces stronger warming per emitted mass over short periods than carbon dioxide, but atmospheric methane is shorter-lived.
false: Methane produces weaker warming per emitted mass over short periods than carbon dioxide and remains in the atmosphere much longer.

true: Active pieces outweigh a small material deficit when immediate threats prevent the opponent from coordinating or consolidating.
false: Active pieces automatically outweigh any material deficit because immediate threats permanently prevent the opponent from coordinating or consolidating.

true: A rook on the seventh rank attacks pawns, restricts the enemy king, and creates threats worth more than passive material.
false: A rook on the seventh rank attacks pawns and restricts the enemy king, guaranteeing compensation for a sacrificed minor piece.

true: An initiative compensates for material only while forcing moves arrive quickly enough to deny the defender time for consolidation.
false: An initiative permanently compensates for material once forcing moves begin, even after the defender gains time for consolidation.

true: An exposed king makes extra material irrelevant when active enemy pieces coordinate a forced mating attack.
false: An exposed king remains safe when its side has extra material, because additional defenders neutralize every coordinated mating attack.

true: An advanced passed pawn compensates for sacrificed material when it ties down defenders and threatens promotion.
false: An advanced passed pawn compensates for sacrificed material whenever promotion remains legally possible, even without restricting any defender.

true: The bishop pair becomes especially active in open positions, where long diagonals allow both bishops to influence opposite-colored squares.
false: The bishop pair becomes especially active in closed positions, where blocked diagonals allow both bishops to influence opposite-colored squares.

true: A positional exchange sacrifice trades a rook for a minor piece to gain lasting activity, structure, or king pressure.
false: A positional exchange sacrifice trades a minor piece for a rook to gain lasting activity, structure, or king pressure.

true: Standard piece values are rough averages; mobility, coordination, pawn structure, king safety, and tactical timing determine practical value.
false: Standard piece values remain exact in every position; mobility, coordination, pawn structure, king safety, and timing cannot alter practical value.

true: Metals bend plastically when dislocations move through nondirectional metallic bonds without immediately separating the crystal.
false: Metals bend plastically when entire atomic planes separate through metallic bonds and then reconnect after deformation.

true: Ceramics shatter with little plastic deformation because strong directional or ionic bonds impede dislocation motion before fracture.
false: Ceramics shatter with little plastic deformation because strong directional or ionic bonds accelerate dislocation motion before fracture.

true: Microscopic flaws concentrate tensile stress in ceramics, driving rapid crack propagation once the local fracture threshold is reached.
false: Microscopic flaws distribute tensile stress throughout ceramics, allowing cracks to propagate rapidly once the average fracture threshold is reached.

true: Plastic deformation around a crack tip absorbs energy and blunts the crack, making many metals relatively tough.
false: Plastic deformation around a crack tip sharpens and accelerates the crack, making many metals relatively tough.

true: In susceptible metals, lower temperatures and faster loading suppress plastic deformation, producing more brittle fracture than warm, slow loading.
false: Lower temperatures and faster loading promote plastic deformation, making metals consistently more ductile than under warm, slow loading.

true: Within the Hall-Petch regime, reducing grain size strengthens a metal because grain boundaries hinder dislocation motion across neighboring crystals.
false: Within the Hall-Petch regime, increasing grain size strengthens a metal because fewer grain boundaries hinder dislocation motion across neighboring crystals.

true: Ceramics withstand compression better than tension because compression closes cracks while tension pulls crack faces apart.
false: Ceramics withstand tension better than compression because tension closes cracks while compression pulls crack faces apart.

true: Cold working raises dislocation density, making further slip harder and increasing metal strength while reducing ductility.
false: Cold working removes dislocations, making further slip harder and increasing metal strength while reducing ductility.

true: A p-value is the probability, assuming the null model, of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed.
false: A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true after obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed.

true: A small p-value measures incompatibility with the null model, not the size or practical importance of the observed effect.
false: A small p-value measures the size and practical importance of the observed effect, not merely incompatibility with the null model.

true: Rejecting a null hypothesis at a chosen threshold does not establish that the alternative explanation is practically important or causal.
false: Rejecting a null hypothesis at a chosen threshold establishes that the alternative explanation is practically important and causal.

true: Failing to reject the null means the data lack sufficient evidence against it, not that the null has been proven true.
false: Failing to reject the null means the data provide sufficient evidence that the null hypothesis has been proven true.

true: With a large sample, a scientifically trivial effect produces a very small p-value when estimation becomes sufficiently precise.
false: With a large sample, only a scientifically important effect produces a very small p-value because sample size removes trivial differences.

true: A p-value is trustworthy only to the extent that the sampling design, statistical model, and test assumptions are appropriate.
false: A p-value remains trustworthy even when sampling design and test assumptions fail because its calculation automatically corrects model errors.

true: Testing many hypotheses without adjustment increases the chance of finding at least one small p-value under true null hypotheses.
false: Testing many hypotheses without adjustment leaves the chance of finding a small p-value unchanged because every test is calculated separately.

true: For a matching two-sided test, a null value outside the corresponding confidence interval is rejected at the associated significance level.
false: For a matching two-sided test, a null value inside the corresponding confidence interval is rejected at the associated significance level.

true: Network latency measures how long data takes to travel, while bandwidth measures the data transferred per unit time.
false: Network latency measures the data transferred per unit time, while bandwidth measures how long each packet takes to travel.

true: A high-bandwidth connection still feels slow for interactive tasks when propagation, routing, or queueing produces high latency.
false: A high-bandwidth connection necessarily feels fast for interactive tasks because increasing capacity proportionally reduces propagation and routing latency.

true: Transferring a large file depends mainly on sustained throughput, while its startup also incurs latency from connection setup and requests.
false: Transferring a large file depends mainly on latency, while sustained throughput matters only during connection setup and requests.

true: Propagation delay comes from distance and signal speed, whereas transmission delay depends on packet size and link bandwidth.
false: Propagation delay depends on packet size and link bandwidth, whereas transmission delay comes from distance and signal speed.

true: A ping primarily estimates round-trip latency and packet loss; it does not directly measure a connection's available bandwidth.
false: A ping primarily estimates available bandwidth from round-trip latency, directly revealing the connection's maximum bulk transfer rate.

true: Video streaming needs enough sustained bandwidth, while online games depend more strongly on low and stable latency.
false: Video streaming depends mainly on low latency, while online games depend more strongly on maximum sustained bandwidth.

true: Congestion increases latency as packets wait in queues and reduces useful throughput through loss, retransmission, or contention.
false: Congestion increases bandwidth as packets accumulate in queues, improving useful throughput through retransmission and contention.

true: TCP throughput remains below link bandwidth when round-trip time, packet loss, or receive-window limits constrain data in flight.
false: TCP throughput always reaches link bandwidth regardless of round-trip time or packet loss because acknowledgments do not constrain data in flight.
